Samegrelo:
Don't get trapped on a sanitized tourist bus when you could be exploring the lush, untamed jungles of Samegrelo. This is a fertile, rolling area where the clearest rivers in Georgia rush down from rugged slopes on their way to the sea. Stepping off the paved roads reveals towering waterfalls and quiet beaches that the mainstream crowds ignore.

The Megrelian people speak their own language and live with an infectious, epicurean enthusiasm. While most tourists eat overpriced, mediocre food in the center of town, our days end around village tables piled high with feasts. Megrelian food is lavishly flavored with the real, raw spices of their gardens, featuring dishes you simply cannot find anywhere else.

The terrain here is broad and diverse, waiting for you to get your boots muddy. We can paddle a rowboat through the massive, pristine swamps of the Kolkheti Reserve where water buffaloes bathe lazily by the seaside. If you crave a genuine physical challenge, the trails leading up to the isolated Tobavarchkhili Lake offer an alpine secret tucked away in the clouds.

I know the hidden secrets of this region because I have driven the dirt roads and walked the forgotten trails. We can explore the clear waters of Balda Canyon or soak in the outdoor hot springs of Nokalakevi. Tell me what kind of adventure you are looking for, and we will hit the dirt to experience the true character of Samegrelo.
Guria:
Most tourists just drive straight through Guria on their way to crowded seacoast resorts, missing out on one of the most charming parts of Georgia. Their loss is your gain. Nestled in the foothills of the Lesser Caucasus, this small, cozy area offers a genuine connection to the local culture. We bypass the sterile tourist traps and step directly into a world of sharp humor and incredibly warm hospitality.

The subtropical climate here is perfect for growing mandarins and unique varieties of grapes. Instead of rushing through a scripted itinerary, we take the time to walk or cycle through peaceful villages and explore small medieval churches like Shemokmedi and Jikheti. When the heat rises, local river swimming holes offer a perfect escape.

For those willing to embrace a little grit, the forested foothills and high mountains to the south offer a completely different reality. Leaving the overbuilt resorts behind, the route ventures into the rolling green peaks where summer herding families manufacture cheese amidst endless wildflower fields. This is the raw, unpolished side of the country that you came to experience.

Guria also produces some of the finest tea west of China, including a fermented mountain blueberry leaf tea that leaves a lasting impression. I have put the miles in to find these authentic experiences so you do not have to guess where the real Georgia hides. Grab your boots, and we will uncover the rugged, off-road beauty of Guria together.
Adjara:
The Adjarian seacoast is heavily overrun by the sanitized tourism industry, filled with concrete skyscrapers and cynical seaside traps. Fortunately, you do not have to settle for that manufactured experience. Just a few steps away from the noise lies the real Adjara: a land of steep, jungle-covered mountains and swift rivers carving through the terrain.

The true character of Adjara is found high in the mountains, not on the crowded beaches. Getting your boots muddy crossing medieval stone bridges is the best way to reach isolated highland villages. The people here are the most openhearted hosts in all of Georgia, ready to welcome guests with a tiny cup of perfectly brewed coffee and a genuine smile.

Highland Adjarians are masterful cheesemakers and beekeepers, taking vast herds of cattle up to the alpine zones every summer. While other travelers eat generic buffet food, our groups sit around tables piled high with feasts of kaymagh creams and tenili string cheese. The mountain floral honey and strong brews of blueberry leaf tea showcase the abundant, raw flavor of the environment.

I know how to bypass the chaos of the coast to bring you safely into these intensely green forests and rolling summer mountains. Whether you prefer hiking through the Mtirala reserves or joining herding families in their wooden cottages, this is a Georgia most people never see. Tell me what kind of untamed adventure you want, and we will leave the tourist bubble far behind.
Lechkhumi:
Lechkhumi is the smallest of the Georgian regions, so obscure that even many locals forget it exists. This means travelers can completely avoid the sanitized tourism industry and step into an untouched, rugged paradise. Enclosed by towering mountains on all sides, this territory is a labyrinth of sheer cliffs and chestnut forests that project a profound, raw reality.

At the center of it all rises Khvamli, a massive limestone cliff wrapped in ancient mysteries and millennia-old mythology. Stepping off the paved routes leads to hidden caves carved with astrological symbols and sweeping views of the Black Sea and Mount Elbrus. This is not a polished museum exhibit; it is a visceral encounter with history earned through muddy boots.

For those who crave real adventure, the steep and forbidding Lechkhumi Ridge offers narrow, trackless trails and desolate beauty. The journey up to Akhalchala reveals a rustic summer village set in a large meadow surrounded by the region's highest peaks. Up here, the pure air and clear mountain streams provide the majestic isolation found only in the truly untamed corners of the world.

Lechkhumi also happens to grow some of the rarest and most delicious grapes in the country, carefully cultivated in small village vineyards. Instead of attending a corporate wine tasting, we share unpretentious, unforgettable vintages with local families who drink far better than anyone in a fancy boutique. I have explored these obscure pathways for years, and I am ready to guide you straight into the hidden secrets of Lechkhumi.
Racha:
Racha shares the spectacular Rioni river valley with its twin region, Lechkhumi, offering a deeply authentic alternative to crowded tourist hotspots. There are no sanitized package tours here. Instead, the river flows wild and swift near its birthplace in the high mountains, setting the unhurried rhythm of village life.

While others rush from one famous landmark to the next, we take the time to explore the quiet grandeur of Racha's historical sites. Standing before the intricate stone carvings of Nikortsminda and the isolated beauty of Mravaldzali brings you face to face with the Great Caucasus. These are places of deep, grounded history appreciated best far from the busy highways.

The high mountains of Upper Racha are an absolute paradise for those willing to put in the physical effort. The trail passes through exquisite pine forests and forgotten wilderness before reaching camp by the pristine, isolated waters of Udziro Lake. This environment demands respect and repays the effort with unfiltered panoramas of the peaks.

I have spent some of my happiest days wandering these valleys, learning the hidden secrets of the karstic caves and towering waterfalls. My job is to handle the logistics so you can simply focus on the dirt under your feet and the incredible scale of the mountains above. Jump in the off-road car, and we will find the cozy, untamed adventures waiting in Racha.
Imereti:
Imereti is a sprawling, decadent land that encompasses stark canyons and fertile plains. Do not settle for the standard day trips that trap travelers in a sanitized bubble. Venturing off the beaten track reveals the true character of this area, from the subterranean rivers of its limestone caves to the spectacular mountain panoramas of the Lesser Caucasus.

The locals here possess a goofy humor and an intense dedication to indulgent gastronomy. While the tourist masses eat generic hotel meals, we pull up chairs to tables piled high with feasts of spiced bean soup and fresh cheese pastries. This is authentic, unpretentious hospitality where the food is deeply rooted in the agricultural reality of the Colchian plain.

The terrain demands to be explored with muddy boots and a healthy sense of curiosity. Hiking through the mystical Rioni valley reveals natural caverns at Tsutskhvati and hidden waterfalls in the Khani valley. Whether driving the winding plateau around Chiatura or climbing to the roof of the region at Zekari pass, the unfettered beauty of the land is undeniable.

I know the hidden secrets of Imereti because I have actually put the miles in to find them. This province rewards those who are willing to embrace a little grit and leave the guidebook behind. Tell me what kind of untamed adventure you are looking for, and we will hit the dirt to uncover everything Imereti has to offer.
Meskheti:
Meskheti is a stark, dramatic region defined by the mighty Mtkvari canyon and the heavy, lingering presence of the Middle Ages. Most tourists hurry out and back on sterile day trips just to snap a photo of the Vardzia cave town before rushing back to the city. We bypass that artificial rush, leaving the crowds behind to explore the massive, forgotten fortresses and ancient tunnels scattered across the desolate plateaus.

This is a place where the history is as rugged as the terrain itself. Hiking up to the ruins of Tmogvi Castle reveals the tangled roots of a 400-year-old grapevine hidden deep in the valley below. There are no velvet ropes here; visitors experience the visceral reality of medieval architecture slowly being reclaimed by the untamed environment.

Beyond the canyon, the misty ridges of the Tori mountains offer an intense, isolated hiking experience free from other travelers. The route tracks through forgotten forests to find unmarked hot springs and the alien-like Stone Man of Uraveli, one of the last surviving pagan idols in the country. This is real exploration, where every discovery feels earned by the sweat on your brow.

I have driven these open steppes and walked these rocky paths to uncover the true character of Meskheti. Traveling with me means eating unique local noodles in authentic village guesthouses and sleeping under the vast, open sky. Grab your boots, and we will head out to find the ancient mysteries that this area holds.
Javakheti:
The Javakheti Plateau is a vast, volcanic expanse defined by extreme elevations and a profound sense of emptiness. Soft, sanitized comforts do not exist here; this is a rugged, hardscrabble environment that demands respect. Leaving the comfortable tourist bubble exposes a land born of fire, where dormant calderas and sprawling alpine lakes dominate the desolate horizon.

The massive lakes of Javakheti are central to life on the plateau, swarming with migratory birds in the summer and freezing inches thick in the harsh winters. Out here, we meet the resilient ethnic Armenians and pacifist Russian Doukhobors who make their living raising potatoes and fishing in these cold waters. This offers a rare opportunity to connect with isolated communities that survive on the very edge of the known world.

For those who want to push their limits, the volcanic peaks provide an otherworldly hiking experience over basalt and pumice. The climb reaches heights over 3,300 meters, stepping over stones to find the monumental Bronze Age megaliths of Abuli and Shaori. These impossible, mortarless structures sit at extreme elevations, offering a visceral connection to a powerful and completely forgotten civilization.

I know the hidden secrets of this plateau because I have spent the time exploring its freezing winds and trackless slopes. My job is to handle the harsh logistics so you can safely experience the majestic isolation and ancient mysteries of Javakheti. Tell me what kind of raw adventure you are seeking, and we will hit the dirt.
Kartli:
Kartli is the historical heartland of Georgia, heavily bypassed by tourists who only stop for a quick museum tour before fleeing to the next generic landmark. Avoiding that superficial trap opens up the most diverse, historically dense area in the country. We explore the vast labyrinth of the Trialeti Range, uncovering forgotten villages and ancient monuments hidden deep in the forests.

The southern marchlands are a raw patchwork of cultures displaying the ruined glory of the Georgian Golden Age. The trails lead to the massive archaeological site of Samshvilde, a city inhabited for six thousand years, before tracking through dense overgrowth to find abandoned Armenian monasteries. This is a place where history is not cordoned off behind glass; it is weathered, overgrown, and waiting to be found.

On the quiet Tsalka plateau, visitors walk among prehistoric standing stones and the remnants of megalithic fortresses. For a true physical adventure, the steep ridges of the Algeti and Tedzami valleys push past old bandit fortresses and peculiarly decorated ancient chapels. The terrain here is fiercely beautiful, demanding muddy boots in exchange for the best panoramic views.

I have driven the off-road trails and hiked the steep canyons of Kartli to map out its most authentic experiences. Whether scaling the dramatic cliffs of the Ateni valley or sitting down with locals in a remote agricultural village, this is a Georgia most people never see. Leave the paved routes behind, and let us uncover the true character of the heartland.
Svaneti:
Svaneti was once a fiercely remote, mountainous stronghold, but today its main towns are rapidly being swallowed by the sanitized tourism industry. There is no need to settle for the concrete hotels and crowded bars that plague the popular centers. Venturing beyond the tourist traps exposes the raw peaks and the beautiful traditions that define the true character of this area.

This is a paradise for those who want to test their endurance against the terrain. The steep, narrow trails connect isolated villages and pass by centuries-old defensive stone towers that still guard the valleys. The mountains here dictate the terms of the journey, rewarding physical effort with unfiltered views of the Greater Caucasus.

The Svans have a deep, complex history, preserving a culture where Christianity and paganism exist together at ancient stone shrines. Inside small, forgotten village churches sit utterly unique medieval frescoes that survived because of the region's historical isolation. This environment feels like a spiritual gateway to a different world, far removed from the sterile tours of the lowlands.

I know how to bypass the logistical chaos of modern Svaneti to get you safely out into the untamed wilderness. We leave the crowds behind to eat real food with local families and get muddy on the high trails. Tell me how deep into the mountains you want to go, and we will find the hidden secrets of Svaneti together.
Mtianeti:
Mtianeti is a vast, forbidding land of fierce rivers and massive peaks that loom overhead and distort your sense of scale. Sanitized comforts do not exist out here; the grip of winter holds these valleys for more than half the year. Traveling into this territory means entering a rugged world where the terrain dictates the terms and ancient mountaineer traditions still hold strong.

This is not a place for casual sightseeing from the window of an air-conditioned bus. The steep trails lead up to places like Khevsureti and Tusheti, where ancient defensive towers spring from the green ridges. The mountaineers who live here are sober, serious folk who maintain stone shrines where old pagan customs flow together with Christian traditions in the shadow of the peaks.

When the brief summer arrives and the high pastures bloom with rhododendrons, the intense isolation sets the mind free. Trekkers can go for days out of the sight of civilization, sleeping in tents or sharing rustic shelter with local herders. Whether crossing the Datvisjvari Pass or fording the rushing rivers of Gudamakari, every step must be earned.

I have spent years exploring these endless, fascinating valleys, and I still feel like there is always another secret waiting over the next ridge. My job is to handle the off-road driving and the tough logistics so you can fully immerse yourself in the raw reality of the mountains. Grab your boots, and we will discover the true, unyielding character of Mtianeti.
Kakheti:
Kakheti is heavily marketed as a generic wine region, filled with massive corporate vineyards and kitschily reconstructed fortress towns built to appease the sanitized tourism industry. We bypass those manufactured experiences entirely. Hitting the dirt roads exposes the wild, untamed nature and the deeply authentic local culture that the big tour companies actively ignore.

The terrain of Kakheti is shockingly diverse and requires muddy boots to fully appreciate. The trails run along the misty ridges of the Gombori Range and push through the dense forests of the Greater Caucasus to reach isolated alpine lakes. In the south, the harsh, dry canyons of the Vashlovani desert offer a profound silence and vast spaces entirely devoid of human traces.

The history here is etched directly into the rugged environment. A short climb leads to ancient cave monasteries carved by hand into the desert cliffs, where vibrant medieval frescoes still cling to the rock faces. Wandering through forgotten forests reveals slowly toppling, moss-covered basilicas that offer a visceral connection to the past, far away from any velvet ropes or ticket booths.

The true soul of Kakheti is found around tables piled high with feasts, not in sterile tasting rooms. We share powerful, funky wines fermented in traditional clay qvevris and eat barbecue roasted over open fires by unpretentious locals. I know the hidden secrets of this massive territory, and I am ready to help you experience the raw, unfiltered reality of Kakheti.
Tbilisi:
Tbilisi is a chaotic, beautiful collision of ancient history and modern construction, where soulless concrete skyscrapers constantly threaten to pave over the city's bohemian soul. We avoid the sterilized, scripted tourist circuits that try to hide the grit. Stepping onto the broken sidewalks reveals the scintillating energy of a true crossroads city built into a dramatic canyon.

The real character of Tbilisi is found in its swarming, serpentine bazaars and its quiet, angular backstreet courtyards. Leaving the main avenues leads to echoing bathhouses and subterranean khinkali dungeons where the locals actually spend their time. Every street here heaves with the memories of the Silk Road, offering chance encounters and raw, unscripted nights.

For those who want to dig deeper into the urban fabric, the outskirts of the city hold their own untamed adventures. The outer suburbs hide abandoned Soviet factories, while the hike up to the ruins of Kojori fortress grants spectacular views of the valley. This is not a polished museum city; it is a living, breathing labyrinth that demands to be explored on foot.

While I usually focus on the wild regions beyond the city limits, I know the hidden secrets of my adopted hometown better than anyone. My job is to point you toward the authentic, unpretentious corners of Tbilisi that never appear in any glossy guidebook. Tell me what kind of urban adventure you are looking for, and we will hit the streets to find the real city.
